Jewish conversion, called giyur, is the formal process by which a non-Jew becomes a member of the Jewish people, adopting Jewish faith, law, and identity. The conversion process requires study of Jewish law and practice, acceptance of the mitzvot—the commandments—and ritual acts including immersion in a mikveh, a ritual bath. Conversion is recognized differently across Jewish denominations, with Orthodox, Conservative, and Reform each establishing their own standards and procedures.

A beit din, a rabbinic court, oversees the conversion process, assessing the sincere motivation and commitment of the person seeking to convert. The convert studies Jewish law, history, theology, and practice with a rabbi or designated instructor, typically over months or even years depending on the depth and thoroughness of the program.

The convert must demonstrate commitment to observing halakha, Jewish law, though what constitutes acceptable observance varies across denominations. Reform Judaism, for instance, may require a lighter commitment than Orthodox Judaism. Ritual immersion in a mikveh is performed with witnesses present, marking the spiritual transformation and entry into the Jewish people. For male converts, brit milah—circumcision—or hatafat dam brit, a ritual drawing of a drop of blood, is performed as part of the conversion process.

The convert receives a Hebrew name, formally establishing Jewish identity. This name is used in all subsequent Jewish religious contexts, just as it would be for someone born Jewish. After conversion is complete, the individual is considered fully Jewish for all purposes. Their status as a Jew is equal to that of someone born into the Jewish people.

However, conversion standards and recognitions differ across movements. Orthodox conversion is not automatically recognized by Reform or Conservative movements, and vice versa, creating practical complications for some converts. A person converted under Reform auspices, for instance, may not be recognized as Jewish by Orthodox authorities. These differences reflect deeper theological and halakhic disagreements among the movements about what conversion requires and what it means.
